claimed.text: Grusch testified that in the course of his official duties he was informed of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme, was denied the read-ons when he asked, and reported this to his superiors and several inspectors general.

He testified that the Task Force Director tasked him in 2019 to identify all relevant special access programmes. The board infers that the director was Jay Stratton; Grusch has never named him on the record.

Asked whether the government possesses UAP, he answered that it does, based on interviewing over 40 witnesses over four years, said he knew the locations and had given them to the Inspector General, and said he had those with first-hand knowledge make their own protected disclosures.

Asked by Rep. Mace, he testified that biologics came with some recoveries and were non-human, which he gave as the assessment of people with direct knowledge still on the programme; he offered her a list of cooperative and hostile witnesses, which has never surfaced.

On funding, he testified to misappropriation and self-funding through contractors' internal research and development money, and said he was not aware of any duty on contractors to report UAP; earlier he had told The Debrief of illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations.
He testified that he has personal knowledge of people harmed in efforts to conceal the technology, and on murder said only that he had directed people with that knowledge to the authorities.

He testified that he gave Sean Kirkpatrick his concerns in a classified conversation in April 2022, before Kirkpatrick led AARO, and that Kirkpatrick's testimony of no credible evidence was not accurate.

His reprisal complaint alleges that his identity and his communications with the DoD Inspector General were disclosed outside that office; Eric Davis has since described three separate acts of harassment against him by different actors.

His later public statements go further than his testimony: he told NewsNation in 2023 that dead pilots are sometimes encountered, and at a Capitol press conference in June 2026 alleged slush funds of billions a year and spoke of several kinds of non-human intelligence known to the government.

Others support him on the record: Karl Nell called him beyond reproach and his account of a reverse-engineering arms race fundamentally correct; Mellon says well-placed officials shared detailed information with him; Luis Elizondo said under oath in 2024 that he agreed with Grusch's testimony; and Leslie Kean said in June 2023 that Garry Nolan knows Grusch well and vouches for him. The board notes that no document establishes whether Mellon's sources and Grusch's overlap.

The board infers two things it cannot document: that the Disclosure Act's definitions of privately held material were drafted in response to his allegations, and that the Department's unauditable ledger, whose FY2025 audit found 26 material weaknesses, cannot disprove the misappropriation claim.

contested.text: The Department's June 2023 answer was that AARO had not discovered any verifiable information substantiating a possession or reverse-engineering programme, which is a statement about AARO's discoveries rather than the Department's knowledge.

AARO's Historical Record Report of March 2024 is the formal answer: it says none of its interviewees had first-hand knowledge, that most claims were inaccurate or misidentified authentic programmes, that it found no empirical evidence of government or private reverse engineering of extraterrestrial technology, and that the claim is largely the product of circular reporting among a group of believers. The board notes that it does not engage Grusch's statement that first-hand witnesses made their own disclosures to the Inspector General.

AARO's central impeachment is that Grusch would not be interviewed; Grusch cites legal and security exposure, and on the board's reading the memorandum records no offer of a venue with the Inspector General or congressional counsel present. The two records of the memorandum also count AARO's approaches differently, eight and nine.

The credible-and-urgent finding attributed to the Inspector General, known on the board only through Grusch's own testimony, and AARO's later finding of no verifiable information and no first-hand knowledge are, on the board's reading, executive-branch determinations on the same allegations that no document reconciles.

AARO's reports address the retrieval claims but say nothing about misappropriated funds, illegal contracting or contractor research money, and his written testimony likewise reserved funding specifics for closed session.

The release of his emergency-custody records is disputed in both directions: Mace calls it a leak of private medical information aimed at him, while a Virginia court held that the redacted police-record release complied with FOIA.
Prepublication clearance is not endorsement: it establishes that DoD read and released his words, and Grusch himself says they are his own views, not the Department's.

lead.text: David Grusch, a former intelligence officer who sat on the UAP Task Force, testified under oath in July 2023 that he was told in his official duties of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering programme he was denied access to, that biologics came with some recoveries and were non-human in the assessment of people he spoke to, that it is funded by misappropriation, and that he suffered retaliation. According to his testimony and The Debrief, the Intelligence Community Inspector General found his complaint credible and urgent; the Department said AARO had found no verifiable information, and AARO says he would not meet it.

record.text: His House Oversight biography records an active top secret clearance, service as the NRO's representative to the UAP Task Force from 2019 to 2021 and as NGA co-lead for UAP analysis; the printed hearing record lists him as a former NRO representative to the Task Force.

Charles McCullough III, the first Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, filed Grusch's urgent-concern disclosure with that office on 25 May 2022. According to Grusch's sworn testimony and The Debrief, the Inspector General found it credible and urgent in July 2022, a finding that obliges transmission to the intelligence committees.

The Defense Office of Prepublication and Security Review cleared his statements for open publication on 4 and 6 April 2023; its internal emails show reviewers discussing his references to sensitive areas and deciding vague references were not a problem. Grusch said under oath that the review was a security review only and that the views were his own.

The Debrief article of 5 June 2023, by Kean and Blumenthal, carried named on-record support from Karl Nell and Christopher Mellon and pseudonymous support from a serving NASIC officer; Kean vetted Grusch through Nell and the NASIC officer.

The House Oversight national security subcommittee heard Ryan Graves, Grusch and David Fravor under oath on 26 July 2023; Burchett opened by recording that members had been denied a SCIF briefing before the hearing.

AARO's memorandum for record, released under FOIA, logs nine contacts or attempts between June 2023 and January 2024, mostly through intermediaries or Senate staff; Grusch agreed to a 14 November 2023 interview in Arlington and did not attend, and declined a later invitation on security grounds. AARO concluded he had no intention of providing it with information.

The same file cites a March 2023 memorandum by Maj. Gen. David Abba, director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office, as the access authority AARO invoked, and an ODNI memorandum affirming AARO's authority to receive classified UAP disclosures.

In August 2023 The Intercept published Loudoun County Sheriff's records of Grusch's 2014 and 2018 emergency custody episodes, obtained by Ken Klippenstein under Virginia FOIA. Grusch sued the Sheriff in July 2024; the suit was dismissed with prejudice on 6 August 2025.

Rep. Eli Crane wrote to the Secretary of Defense on 24 July 2025 that Grusch had lost his clearance, a promotion and his medical retirement in reprisal, and entered the letter into the record of the Task Force hearing of 9 September 2025, saying he had had no reply.

Grusch's biography lists him as chief operating officer of the Sol Foundation, co-founded by Garry Nolan, from May 2023, and Burlison's office announced in March 2025 that Grusch's adviser role includes service on the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets.

The Senate-passed text of the UAP Disclosure Act (S. 2226 as engrossed) defines a legacy programme to include private efforts to exploit technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of non-human intelligence, and the statute Grusch cited on special access programme waivers exists with the waiver provision he described.

summary.text: The route to the public: an urgent-concern complaint filed with the Intelligence Community Inspector General in May 2022 through counsel, which by Grusch's sworn account and The Debrief's was found credible and urgent that July; prepublication clearance of his statements in April 2023; a Debrief article by Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal on 5 June 2023; and sworn testimony to House Oversight on 26 July 2023.

The allegations fall into four strands: a concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering programme, non-human biologics, funding by misappropriation and contractor research money, and reprisal against him for reporting it.

By his own account his knowledge is second-hand: he says his account rests on interviews with over 40 witnesses over four years, some of whom made their own protected disclosures. On-record supporters include Karl Nell and Christopher Mellon, who describes his own sources separately.

In March 2025 he was hired for a four-month term as an adviser to Rep. Eric Burlison, and a July 2026 directive reported to waive UAP-related nondisclosure agreements for witnesses speaking to authorised investigators addresses, on the board's reading, the barrier he described.
